blocks.text: (2) The Middle Stage of the Highest Grade

inline.s: As for those of the middle stage of the highest grade: they need not uphold and recite the Vaipulya scriptures; but they well understand the meaning and drift, are not disturbed in mind regarding the first principle, deeply believe in cause and effect, and do not slander the Mahayana. With this merit they dedicate it, and vow to seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

As for those of the middle stage of the highest grade: they need not uphold and recite the Mahayana scriptures; but they well understand the meaning and drift of the Buddha's teaching, are not disturbed in mind regarding the first principle, deeply believe in cause and effect, and do not slander the Mahayana. With this merit they dedicate it, and vow to seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Not needing to uphold and recite the Vaipulya scriptures: The Wondrous Axiom Commentary (the Wondrous Axiom Commentary on the Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, Song
dynasty, a commentary-rendering by the monk Zhili of Siming) says:
'By not needing, it refers to a person who holds to the meaning
(a person who delights in deeply investigating the meaning)
, and does not delight in recitation. He takes but one line or one verse from the scripture and deeply exhausts its purport. Regarding the deep and vast principle that transcends speech and thought
(concerning the deep and vast principle that transcends speech and thought)

, his mind is not disturbed. Moreover, his mind abides in the middle way and is not disturbed by either of the two extremes. He clearly understands that cause and effect are all true reality, and this is called deep faith. Though he has not studied exhaustively, if he hears the great teaching or its differing explanations given in accord with capacities, he knows that they reveal a single principle, and he gives rise to no doubt or slander.'

The middle way: nowhere leaning toward emptiness, nowhere leaning toward existence; neither empty nor existent, yet both empty and existent; not falling into either of the two extremes; perfectly interfused and unobstructed — this is called the middle way.
The first principle: the supreme, perfect, and ultimate truth. The true reality of all dharmas is the first principle. The Buddha said:

All dharmas are wholly false and illusory; wherever they cease, that is called true, that is called true reality, that is called the Dharma realm, that is called ultimate wisdom, that is called the truth of the first principle, that is called the emptiness of the first principle.
The first principle is also called the truth of the first principle. 'Truth' means the principle that is true and without error.
(from the Great Parinirvana Sutra
, chapter forty.) The true reality of all dharmas: this is the actual condition of all dharmas. The Buddha Repository Sutra says:
What is called the true reality of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty, entirely without existence.
The Great Parinirvana Sutra says:
All dharmas are like illusory appearances; the Tathagata, within them, through the power of skill-in-means, is not attached to anything.
The Lotus Sutra says:
The bodhisattva-mahasattva contemplates all dharmas as empty, as true reality, without inversion, without agitation, without regression, without turning.
For a detailed discussion of the true reality of all dharmas, see
The True Reality of All Dharmas
article.

When a person who practices this is about to end his life, Amitabha Buddha, together with Avalokitesvara, Mahasthamaprapta, and surrounded by the measureless great assembly and retinue, comes bearing a purple-golden throne to the practicer and praises him, saying: 'Dharma-son, you practice the Mahayana and understand the first principle; therefore I now come to welcome you.' Together with a thousand transformation Buddhas, they extend their hands at the same moment.

When one who practices this is about to end his life, Amitabha Buddha, together with Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva and Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva and surrounded by the measureless great assembly and retinue, comes bearing a purple-golden throne to the practicer and praises him, saying: 'Dharma-son, you practice the Mahayana and understand the first principle; therefore I now come to welcome you.' Together with a thousand transformation Buddhas, they extend their hands to welcome him at the same moment.
Dharma-son: one who follows the Buddha's Way and is nourished by the Dharma.

The practicer sees himself seated on the purple-golden throne, with palms together and hands clasped, praising the Buddhas. In the space of a single thought he is born in the pond of the seven treasures of that land. This purple-golden throne is like a great jeweled flower that opens after a single night. The practicer's body becomes the color of pure gold, and beneath his feet there are likewise lotus flowers of the seven treasures. The Buddha and the bodhisattvas all emit light, shining upon the practicer's body, and his eyes immediately open and grow clear.

The practicer sees himself seated on the purple-golden throne, with palms together and hands clasped, praising the Buddhas. In the space of a single thought he is born in the pond of the seven treasures of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. This purple-golden throne is like a great jeweled flower that opens after a single night. The practicer's body becomes the color of pure gold, and beneath his feet there are likewise lotus flowers of the seven treasures. The Buddha and the bodhisattvas all emit light, shining upon the practicer's body, and his eyes immediately open and grow clear, so that he sees the Buddha distinctly.

Clasping the hands: a method of reverent salutation in India, also called the adamant palms together. It is bringing the palms together and crossing the fingers of both hands. The eyes immediately open and grow clear: the eyes immediately open and grow clear, and one sees the Buddha distinctly. Later, in the passage on the lowest stage of the highest grade, it says that one must pass twenty-one days before seeing the Buddha distinctly. The scripture says:

After one day and one night the lotus opens, and within seven days one comes to see the Buddha. Though one sees the Buddha's body, one's mind is not yet clear regarding the many excellent marks; only after twenty-one days does one see him distinctly.

Because of the habits formed in past lives, he universally hears all the voices, purely proclaiming the deep first principle. He then descends from the golden throne, bows to the Buddha, clasps his palms together, and praises the World-Honored One. After seven days he immediately attains non-retrogression with respect to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. He is at once able to fly to the ten directions, passing before the Buddhas and cultivating all the samadhis at the abodes of the Buddhas. After one small kalpa he attains the patient endurance of the unproduced and receives the prophecy in person. This is called one of the middle stage of the highest grade.

Because of the habits formed in past lives, he universally hears all the sounds, all proclaiming the deep first principle. He then descends from the purple-golden throne, bows to the Buddha, clasps his palms together, and praises the World-Honored One. After seven days he immediately attains non-retrogression with respect to Buddha wisdom (anuttara-samyak-sambodhi). He is at once able to fly to the ten directions, making offerings to the Buddhas and cultivating all kinds of samadhi at the abodes of the Buddhas. After one small kalpa he attains the patient endurance of the unproduced and, before each Buddha in turn, receives the prophecy. This is called one of the middle stage of the highest grade. One small kalpa: the human lifespan, beginning at eighty-four thousand years, decreases by one year every hundred years until it reaches ten years; then, starting from ten years, it increases by one year every hundred years until it returns to the original eighty-four thousand years. One such decrease and increase constitutes a small kalpa. It is equal to sixteen million, seven hundred and ninety-eight thousand years.

Because of the habits formed in past lives: because of the habits of past lives in well understanding the meaning and drift, in being undisturbed in mind regarding the first principle, in deeply believing in cause and effect, and in not slandering the Mahayana. Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi: the name of Buddha wisdom, translated into Chinese as the supreme right and perfect enlightenment — that is, the supreme wisdom that truly and equally realizes all truth.

Those of the highest stage of the highest grade, upon being reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, see the Buddha immediately; but those of the middle stage of the highest grade must wait for the purple-golden throne, like a great jeweled flower, to open after a night before they see the Buddha. The former, in a moment, pass before the Buddhas; the latter require seven days. The former receive the prophecy from the Buddhas immediately; the latter require a small kalpa before attaining the patient endurance of the unproduced and the prophecy of the Buddhas.

blocks.text: (3) The Lowest Stage of the Highest Grade

inline.s: As for those of the lowest stage of the highest grade: they likewise believe in cause and effect, do not slander the Mahayana, and only awaken the mind of the supreme Way. With this merit they dedicate it, and vow to seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

As for those of the lowest stage of the highest grade: they likewise believe in cause and effect, do not slander the Mahayana, and only awaken the conviction and resolve to seek the supreme Way. Moreover, with this merit they dedicate it, and vow to seek rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

The mind of the supreme Way: the conviction and resolve to vow to seek the supreme Way. The supreme Way: the Way attained by the Tathagata, beyond which there is nothing higher, and so it is called the supreme Way. The Skillful Means chapter of the Lotus Sutra says:
Uprightly setting aside the skillful means, he solely proclaims the supreme Way.
The Lifespan chapter says:
He always thinks thus: by what means may I cause sentient beings to enter the supreme Way and quickly accomplish the Buddha body?
The chapter on Encouraging the Practice says:
I do not cherish my body and life; I only cherish the supreme Way.

For those of the middle stage of the highest grade, the distinguishing practice is to understand the truth of the first principle. For those of the lowest stage of the highest grade, the distinguishing practice is solely to awaken the mind of the supreme Way.

When that practicer is about to end his life, Amitabha Buddha, together with Avalokitesvara, Mahasthamaprapta, and the various retinue, bearing golden lotus flowers, transform into five hundred transformation Buddhas and come to welcome this person. The five hundred transformation Buddhas extend their hands at the same moment and praise him, saying: 'Dharma-son, you are now pure, and have awakened the mind of the supreme Way; I have come to welcome you.'

When this practicer is about to end his life, Amitabha Buddha, together with Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva, Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva, and the various retinue, bearing golden lotus flowers, transform into five hundred transformation Buddhas and come to welcome him. The five hundred transformation Buddhas extend their hands at the same moment and praise him, saying: 'Dharma-son, you are now pure, and have awakened the mind of the supreme Way; I have come to welcome you.'

When he sees this, he immediately sees his own body seated on a golden lotus flower; once seated, the flower closes, and he follows after the World-Honored One and is reborn in the pond of the seven treasures. After one day and one night the lotus opens, and within seven days he comes to see the Buddha. Though he sees the Buddha's body, his mind is not clear regarding the many excellent marks; only after twenty-one days does he see him distinctly.

When this practicer sees this (the Buddhas and bodhisattvas coming to welcome him), he immediately sees his own body seated on a golden lotus flower; once seated, the golden lotus closes, and he follows after the World-Honored One and is reborn in the pond of the seven treasures of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Only after one day and one night does the golden lotus open, and within seven days he comes to see the Buddha. Though he sees the Buddha's body, his mind is not clear regarding the various excellent marks of the Buddha; only after twenty-one days does he see him distinctly.

He hears the sounds of the assembly, all proclaiming the wondrous Dharma. He travels throughout the ten directions, making offerings to all the Buddhas, and before the Buddhas he hears the deep Dharma. After three small kalpas he attains the understanding gate of the hundred dharmas and abides in the ground of joy. This is called one of the lowest stage of the highest grade.

He universally hears all the sounds, all proclaiming the wondrous Dharma of the supreme Way. Thus he travels throughout the ten directions, making offerings to all the Buddhas, and before the Buddhas he hears the deep Dharma. After three small kalpas he attains the understanding gate of the hundred dharmas and abides in the ground of joy. This is called one of the lowest stage of the highest grade.

The understanding gate of the hundred dharmas: the gate of wisdom that a bodhisattva attains in the first ground (the ground of joy), through which he can penetrate the true nature of the hundred dharmas. The hundred dharmas: also called the hundred dharmas of the five categories; they comprehensively encompass all things in the universe. The five categories: mind dharmas, mental-factors dharmas, form dharmas, dharmas not corresponding with mind, and unconditioned dharmas. The hundred dharmas: mind dharmas number eight and are the self-nature of consciousness; mental-factors dharmas number fifty-one and belong to consciousness; form dharmas number eleven and are transformations of the mind dharmas and mental-factors dharmas; dharmas not corresponding with mind number twenty-four and are the categories of the mind dharmas, mental-factors dharmas, and form dharmas, being also dharmas that correspond neither with mind nor with form; unconditioned dharmas number six. Altogether they form a hundred dharmas.

The ten grounds: among the fifty-two stages of the bodhisattva's practice, the fifth group of ten stages is called the ten grounds. Through these ten grounds one gradually opens the Buddha realm and accomplishes the wisdom of all species; being already on the stage of sages, it is also called the ten sages. First, the ground of joy: when the bodhisattva has fulfilled the practice of the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa, first glimpses the mind-nature, breaks through the delusion of views, and realizes the emptiness of the two (self and dharmas), accomplishes the perfection of giving, and gives rise to great joy — hence it is called the ground of joy. Second, the ground of freedom from defilement: the bodhisattva cuts off the delusion of thought, removes the offense of transgression, makes his body pure, accomplishes the perfection of precepts, and is free from all defilement — hence it is called the ground of freedom from defilement. Third, the ground of radiating light: the bodhisattva extinguishes the darkness of ignorance and attains the three insights, accomplishes the perfection of patience, and the light of his mind shines forth — hence it is called the ground of radiating light. Fourth, the ground of flaming wisdom: the bodhisattva is completely endowed with the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, further cultivates the powers, the fearlessnesses, and the dharmas not shared with others, and, far from idleness, accomplishes the perfection of vigor, so that the flame of his wisdom burns brightly — hence it is called the ground of flaming wisdom. Fifth, the ground of supreme difficult conquest: for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, the bodhisattva studies the various arts externally while within he accomplishes the perfection of meditation; it is supremely difficult to overcome — hence it is called the ground of supreme difficult conquest. Sixth, the ground of presence: the bodhisattva dwells in the method of liberation, cultivates the samadhi of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, accomplishes the perfection of wisdom, and causes all differing appearances present before him to be utterly dissolved — hence it is called the ground of presence. Seventh, the ground of far going: the bodhisattva cuts off the fine manifestations of the fruits of karma, rises to supreme practice, broadly transforms sentient beings, accomplishes the perfection of skill-in-means, and prepares the provisions for the far journey — hence it is called the ground of far going. Eighth, the ground of immovability: the bodhisattva dwells in the patient endurance of the unproduced, cuts off all his previous activities, his body and mind are as still as empty space, and he accomplishes the perfection of vows; with a mind akin to nirvana, he is serene and unmoving — hence it is called the ground of immovability. Ninth, the ground of good wisdom: the bodhisattva extinguishes the marks of mind, realizes the freedom of wisdom, is fully endowed with the ten powers, and clearly knows all places and non-places; he accomplishes the perfection of power and skillfully applies understanding — hence it is called the ground of good wisdom. Tenth, the ground of the Dharma cloud: the bodhisattva broadly gathers measureless Dharma, increases boundless merit and wisdom, knows completely the mind-action of all sentient beings, and according to their superior, middling, and inferior faculties, teaches them the three vehicles; he accomplishes the perfection of wisdom, and like a great cloud, rains the great Dharma rain — hence it is called the ground of the Dharma cloud. The fifty-two stages: from an ordinary being to Buddhahood, the bodhisattva passes altogether through fifty-two stages, namely: the ten faiths, the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten dedications of merit, the ten grounds, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment.

With regard to seeing the Buddha when the flower opens: those of the highest stage of the highest grade see him at once when the time comes; those of the middle stage of the highest grade see him only after a night; those of the lowest stage of the highest grade see him only within seven days, and only after twenty-one days can they see him clearly.
This is called the contemplation of rebirth in the upper class, known as the fourteenth contemplation.

The contemplation of the above three aspects of rebirth (the aspect of the highest stage of the highest grade, the middle stage, and the lowest stage) is together called the contemplation of rebirth in the upper class, known as the fourteenth contemplation.

blocks.text: 15. The Contemplation of the Middle Grade of Rebirth (the assembly of sravakas)
(1) The Highest Stage of the Middle Grade

inline.s: The Buddha told Ananda and Queen Vaidehi: As for those of the highest stage of the middle grade: if any sentient being upholds the five precepts, observes the eight precepts of the fast, practices the various precepts, commits none of the five heinous offenses, and has no excess of faults and evil, then with these roots of goodness he dedicates them and vows to seek rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

The Buddha told Ananda and Queen Vaidehi: As for those of the highest stage of the middle grade: if any sentient being upholds the five precepts, observes the eight precepts of the one-day fast, practices the various precepts, commits none of the five heinous offenses, and has no excess of faults and evil, then with these roots of goodness he dedicates them and vows to seek rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

The five precepts: not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not speaking falsely, and not drinking alcohol. First, not killing — not destroying the lives of sentient beings; second, not stealing — not taking the property of others; third, not committing sexual misconduct — not engaging in sexual acts apart from those between husband and wife; fourth, not speaking falsely — not uttering deceitful, misleading words; fifth, not drinking alcohol — not consuming intoxicating liquors or drugs. The five heinous offenses: these are five kinds of crimes supremely contrary to reason — killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing an arhat, causing blood to flow from the Buddha's body, and causing a schism in the Sangha. Because these five are acts of extreme evil, and the commission of any one of them leads to the avici hell, they are also called the 'avici karma.'

When the practicer is about to end his life, Amitabha Buddha, surrounded by the assembly of monks and his retinue, emitting golden light, comes to the place where this person is, and proclaims suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self, and praises leaving the household life and attaining release from all suffering.
